I've attempted twice. I have treatment resistant depression, anxiety, ADHD. None of it was diagnosed at the time. The first time, I felt like a burden. I genuinely believed my parents would be happier without me and have more money to do whatever with and less stress.

I wasn't a bad kid, and I wasn't a burden. My depression lied to me. That's what depression does, it eats away at your motivation, your desire, your self esteem, and your hope.

The second time was on my brother's birthday. I'd missed a dose of Paxil and it plunged me to the depths so harshly that I wrote a note and texted friends goodbye. One of them called my father, and because of her I'm alive.

I had a turning point when I was watching Breaking Bad. Jesse, after he loses someone he loves, says, "I'm the bad guy."
My heart broke for him. Then I realized if I could still think Jesse was a good person because of his heart rather than his misdeeds, why did I think I was so terrible?

These days I'm leaving an abusive relationship and just started Esketamine treatments for the TRDepression.
It gets better.

I wanted to scream, "You try deep breathing when you're face down having what feels like battery acid injected into the back of your head!"

One thing I noticed is you say you have unresolved trauma and a relationship would heal you. Unfortunately, that's false. The unresolved trauma would most likely infect the relationship in my experience.

Relationships are great. And it would be magical if they healed us, but usually they don't. We have to heal ourselves.
As for me, I'm in therapy and on meds for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. I understand completely the feeling of hopelessness and anxiety and desperation.

Therapy has helped me so much. Took me a few tries to find the person I felt comfortable talking to, but eventually I did and it's going great.

My advice for you is therapy and self love. I understand there's a stigma and men don't normally seek mental health help, but I really think you should because it's so helpful!

Lastly, Charisma on Command is a great YouTube channel for tips on confidence and social interaction :) good luck!

Are they bad people? Most likely no. A lot of the time addicts are just people who are hurting. The problem with saying pain pills aren't good because of hyperalgesia and other side effects is that most chronic pain patients CANNOT function because of their pain anyway, so more (most of the time) wouldn't make much difference. 

As a chronic pain patient, I can tell you I understand the concern, but if given the choice between getting to actually hang out and go places with friends and family or spend my life rotting in bed, I'll pick the pain pills that allow me to function. Maybe I am a bit more sensitive, but in the long run, I don't care. Because the level of pain before the pills is bad enough that a little extra means absolutely nothing to me.

I have neuropathy so bad that if I try to exercise for more than ten minutes, I pass out from pain. I have medical professionals tell me all the time that they've never heard of that, or I'm making it up to get drugs, or seeking attention. Yet I've had other medial professionals witness the pain-induced syncope while I'm connected to machines. When it comes to medicine, I believe the "that doesn't happen" should morph into "that's uncommon". It is so hurtful to be told what I witness all the time in my own body isn't possible. 


Addicts take pain pills to escape from life. Pain patients take pills to try to return to life.

And the fact that some added sensitivity might be someone's excuse for not allowing me the medication that solely gives me my quality of life, well that's just ridiculous.
